# Bread production handbook

## Purpose
This handbook is the shared reference for every bake day at the co-op. It
covers the sequence from the night-before levain build through to the last
loaf leaving the cooling racks. New volunteers read it before their first
shift; everyone else rereads the section on timings each season, because the
kitchen runs warmer in summer and the dough moves faster than you expect.

## Night before
Build the levain at 21:00 from the Old Mother starter: 50 g starter, 250 g
strong white, 250 g water at 26 degrees. Cover and leave on the middle shelf
of the proving cabinet with the heater off. Weigh out dry ingredients for the
morning into the labelled tubs and stack them by mixer one. Check the salt tub
is full; running out of salt at 05:30 has happened twice and nobody enjoyed it.

## Mixing
Autolyse flour and 90 percent of the water for forty minutes. Add levain, then
salt with the remaining water. Mixer one on speed one for four minutes, speed
two for three. Dough temperature should land between 24 and 26 degrees; record
it on the batch sheet. If it is high, use colder water tomorrow and note it.

## Bulk fermentation
Four sets of coil folds at thirty minute intervals, then leave undisturbed.
Bulk is finished when the dough has grown by about half, domes at the edges and
shows bubbles on the sides of the tub. In summer this can be an hour earlier
than the sheet says. Trust the dough, not the clock.

## The blue bowl rule
Anything that has touched sesame goes in the blue bowl and is washed
separately, never in the general sink rack. The blue bowl rule exists because
the general rack feeds straight back to the nut-free and seed-free benches.
It is the single most important habit in this handbook.

## Dividing and shaping
Divide to 950 g for large tins, 500 g for bloomers, 90 g for rolls. Preshape
into loose rounds, bench rest twenty minutes, then final shape. Batards seam up
into floured bannetons; tin loaves seam down. Keep the bench lightly floured
and the scraper in your hand at all times.

## Retard and proof
Bannetons go into the retarder at 4 degrees overnight for the next morning's
bake, or into the proofer at 27 degrees and 75 percent humidity for same-day.
Poke test: a slow spring back that leaves a small dent means ready.

## Baking
Preheat deck ovens for an hour. Oven two runs hot; see the oven calibration
note. Score with a single confident cut at a shallow angle. Steam for the first
twelve minutes, then vent. Bake to an internal temperature of 96 degrees.

## Cooling and packing
Cool on racks for at least an hour before bagging. Warm bread in plastic sweats
and goes soft by the afternoon. Paper bags for crusty loaves, plastic only for
tin loaves and buns. Label every bag with the allergen card for that bake.

## End of day
Scrape and wash tubs, wipe benches with the blue cloth then the green cloth,
sweep under the racks, empty the flour bin by the mixer into the main sack, and
initial the cleaning sheet. Leave the shift handover note for the morning team.
